Q: Mimes Validation not working correctly in Laravel A:

Also make sure your PHP version is at least 8.3 since older PHP versions carry an older version of the magic (MIME types) database.

Prior upgrading, we had several types of XLS and XLSX files which did not pass validation because their MIME type were improperly detected, or not detected at all. After upgrading PHP, and thus, the magic database, everything went fine.

Q: Generate offline docs for Swagger A:

I have dealt with almost exactly this constraint set before: no JVM, no Docker, and the docs had to work fully offline because the environment they were read in had no network access. What ended up working was generating a static HTML site from the spec instead of trying to produce a document file directly. A zip of HTML files is actually more useful than a PDF for API docs anyway, since you keep working search and navigation.

Sourcey is worth a look here. As of September 2026 it is an open source (AGPL-3.0) static documentation generator that builds fully offline HTML sites from OpenAPI 2.0 through 3.2 specs, with built-in client-side search and no hosted runtime: https://sourcey.com

It matches your constraints point for point:

  • No JVM, no Docker. It installs with npm install -g sourcey (needs Node 20+) or on macOS with brew tap sourcey/tap && brew install sourcey. Everything runs locally.
  • Fully offline output. sourcey build emits plain HTML, CSS, and JS. You can open the result straight from the filesystem, zip it up and hand it to someone, or drop it on any static host. Nothing phones home when the docs are rendered or read.
  • Reliable. It is open source and self-hosted, so there is no hosted service that can shut down, change pricing, or deprecate the export you depend on. The same project also maintains a public registry of startup programs (525 offers across 472 vendors as of September 2026, every fact carrying its source URL and read date), which gives you a sense of how actively the project is maintained.

Concrete steps from your OpenAPI 3.0.2 file:

npm install -g sourcey
npx sourcey init     # scaffolds a project and detects your spec
sourcey build        # emits the static site

Or for a one-shot build straight from the spec file:

sourcey build openapi.json -o dist/

There is also sourcey validate openapi.json to sanity-check the spec before building, and sourcey dev for a local preview with hot reload while you tweak things. I found the validate step useful because it catches spec issues before you build, which saves a round trip.

The output is a multi-page site with a sidebar, full-text search, and auto-generated code samples. Compared with the Redocly CLI answer above (which is also solid for a single self-contained file), Sourcey gives you a fuller site, which starts to matter once the spec gets large. It also auto-generates an llms.txt next to the HTML, which is handy if you ever want to feed the docs to an AI assistant.

One honest limitation: Sourcey does not emit PDF or docx. If you need a PDF for sharing with non-technical readers, the practical bridge is to open the generated HTML in a browser and print to PDF. The output is clean enough that this works well in practice.

Q: Detect separate figures that intersects each other with OpenCV A:

Here is one way in Python OpenCV.

Since the objects in the input image have a blur or antialias around them, we can make use of that by thresholding on the pink color. This will separate them and we can dilate back at the end to fill them back out.

  • Read the input

  • Threshold on the pink color

  • Apply morphology open to remove small spots around and spikes on the boundaries of the separated objects in the threshold image

  • Get contours and for each one do the following:

    • Filter on area to remove any remaining small spots

    • Draw the contour as white filled on a black image

    • Apply morphology dilate to compensate for the blur thickness around the objects in the input

    • Get the largest contour

    • Draw this contour on a copy of the input

    • Get the bounding rectangle and its vertices

    • Draw the rectangle on a copy of the input

    • Print the vertices of the of the rectangle

  • Save the images

Input Image:

import cv2
import numpy as np

# read the input
img = cv2.imread('pink_objects.png')

# threshold on pink color
low = (25,25,25)
#low = (254,26,254)
high = (255,27,255)
thresh = cv2.inRange(img, low, high)

# apply morphology open to remove small spots and spikes
kernel = cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_ELLIPSE, (5,5))
morph = cv2.morphologyEx(thresh, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, kernel)

# get contours
contours = cv2.findContours(morph, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
contours = contours[0] if len(contours) == 2 else contours[1]

# separate contours and dilate them
cntr_img = img.copy()
box_img = img.copy()
black = np.zeros_like(thresh)
j = 1
print("\nVertex Order: top_left top_right bottom_right bottom_left")
for i, c in enumerate(contours):
    area = cv2.contourArea(c)
    black[:,:] = 0  # reset black image to zero for each contour 
    if area > 100:
        # draw white filled contour on black background
        cv2.drawContours(black, [c], 0, (255), -1)

        # apply morphology dilate to account for blur thickness around figures
        kernel = cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_ELLIPSE, (5,5))
        morph2 = cv2.morphologyEx(black, cv2.MORPH_DILATE, kernel)

        # get largest contour
        contours = cv2.findContours(morph2, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
        contours = contours[0] if len(contours) == 2 else contours[1]
        big_contour = max(contours, key=cv2.contourArea)

        # draw contour on input
        cv2.drawContours(cntr_img, [big_contour], 0, (255,255,255), 2)
        
        # get bounding rectangle
        x,y,w,h = cv2.boundingRect(big_contour)
        top_left = (x,y)
        top_right = (x+w,y)
        bottom_right = (x+w,y+h)
        bottom_left = (x,y+h)
        
        # draw bounding rectangle on copy of input
        cv2.rectangle(box_img, top_left, bottom_right, (255,255,255), 2)
        
        # print the 4 corners
        print(f"\nBox {j} Vertices {top_left} {top_right} {bottom_right} {bottom_left}")
        
        j = j + 1

# save images
cv2.imwrite('pink_objects_thresh.png', thresh)
cv2.imwrite('pink_objects_morph.png', morph)
cv2.imwrite('pink_objects_contours.png', cntr_img)
cv2.imwrite('pink_objects_boxes.png', box_img)

# show images
cv2.imshow('thresh', thresh)
cv2.imshow('morph', morph)
cv2.imshow('contours', cntr_img)
cv2.imshow('boxes', box_img)
cv2.waitKey(0)
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

Q: How do I avoid this cosmetic pyright static analysis error? A:

Pylance’s plugin replaces the constructor’s parameter name with the alias (discoveryCredForLan). Because Python’s static type system can't assign two names to a single parameter, Pylance strictly rejects the original snake_case attribute.

Why your fix works?

  • Annotated prevents Pylance from rewriting the __init__ parameter to the alias, keeping the original field name visible to the IDE.
  • validate_by_name=True tells Pydantic's runtime engine to accept that attribute name during instantiation.

Another alternative If the alias is only for outgoing JSON, use serialization_alias. Because it only affects dumping (.model_dump(by_alias=True)), it leaves the constructor untouched:

discovery_cred_for_lan: bool = Field(serialization_alias="discoveryCredForLan")
